newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss report says N Korean food situation worse.
newsitem.headline: Swiss report says N Korean food situation worse.

text.p: A Swiss disaster expert has reported that food shortages in disaster-hit North Korea are getting worse, hitting especially children, women and old people, the Foreign Ministry said on Monday.

The report was filed to the Ministry in Berne just before the head of Switzerland's official foreign aid body left for a five-day visit to the Asian communist state to assess needs for further food deliveries and humanitarian assistance.

Spokesman Marco Cameroni said the expert, who has been in North Korea since July 1 and is to stay for a year, had clearly sent the report after visiting a badly-hit area of the north, before rain began falling in some regions at the weekend.
Aid officials last week said millions of North Korean children were suffering from malnutrition and that the crisis was reaching the scale of the Somali and Ethiopian famines of the 1980s.

The foreign aid official, Walter Fust, will tour parts of the country hit by devastating floods two years in a row and now facing the consequences of the prolonged drought, as well as meeting senior North Korean officials.

Fust is director of the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC), through which the Berne government has been funnelling bilateral aid, including food and seed, to the Asian communist state since 1995.

The Foreign Ministry said Swiss aid over the past two years provided directly and through United Nations agencies operating in North Korea -- widely reported as on the brink of famine -- had totalled nearly 11 million Swiss francs ($7.3 million).

The disaster relief expert, a member of a highly-trained team often sent by Switzerland to countries suffering natural disasters, is to provide constant updates on aid needs and logistical support for deliveries.
North Korea's official radio reported on Sunday that more than 100 mm (4 inches) of rain had fallen in some of the worst-hit regions, bringing some relief after the worst heatwave in 61 years.

International relief agencies say the drought caused by the heatwave has increased the likelihood that there would be another disastrous shortfall in the harvest for main crops like rice, maize and corn due in October.

A senior official of the British Red Cross, just back from a visit to the country, said at the weekend that the harvest looked like totalling only 3.3 million (metric) tons, while the country needed 7.4 million tons to meet all needs.

Speaking hours after returning from the region, the body's international director Geoffrey Dennis said North Korea needed the harvest to yield at least 4.3 million tons, "an absolute necessity to feed the population at subsistence level".

Devastating floods in 1995 and 1996 washed away a substantial portion of North Korea's crop acreage, pushing the long secretive state and its 23 million people to the brink of famine, according to foreign and national officials.

North Korea, which maintains a strongly authoritarian political system, has itself reported at least 130 deaths of starving children and allowed international agencies to film malnourished infants in playschools and hospitals.
On Thursday, the United Nations food aid agency appealed to Western countries to give more aid to North Korea to meet a shortfall of up to 800,000 tons of food.
